about: Winaldum (Wijnaldum) in Westergo: one port, written 6 October 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not attested; the landing, the cross and every named person are the game's.

ports.summary: Seven house mounds in a row on a salt-marsh ridge in Westergo, two days north of Dorestad by the Almere and the Vlie. The gold of its old lords is a hundred and fifty years in the ground; in 793 it is a rich farm terp under the Frankish king, with a smith, weavers, a bead bench and more sheep than people. A merchant comes for Frisian cloth, cheese, hides and stock, and brings grain, Rhenish pots and glass, iron and antler, because the terp country grows no bread of its own.
ports.seasons: Shearing after Easter, cloth off the looms from midsummer to Martinmas, and the cattle killed and salted at Martinmas. From the first autumn gales the marsh floods between the mounds and a boat can lie against the terp itself; in a hard winter the creek freezes and the children go out on skates of bone (after 850).

history.text: About this year a great gold brooch set with more than three hundred garnets is worn on the terp, and a goldsmith works there with touchstones and a die for patterned foil.
history.source: Besteman, Bos, Heidinga, Paleo-aktueel 4 (1993); Prummel et al., JALC 3 (2011)

history.text: About this year small silver pennies of the kind called series D are struck in Frisia, possibly on this terp (?).
history.source: Metcalf and Op den Velde, Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 96 (2009)

history.text: This year Charles, the Franks' leader, beat the Frisians on the Boorne, took the land between Vlie and Lauwers and burned the shrines.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Slag aan de Boorne, after the Continuations of Fredegar (?)

history.text: About this year Liudger was sent to break the shrines of the Frisians and brought back the treasure found in them; the king took two thirds. No shrine is named: that one stood at Winaldum is the game's (?).
history.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.16 (ed. Diekamp 1881), by way of spine.json

history.text: About this year the Frisians' law was written down for the king. Between Lauwers and Vlie three new pennies make a solidus; a noble's life is eighty solidi, a free man's fifty-three and a penny.
history.source: Lex Frisionum I (Herold 1557; K. Nieuwenhuijsen's translation, keesn.nl)

history.text: This year two hundred Danish ships lay on the Frisian islands. Three fights were lost and a hundred pounds of silver paid.
This year, on the day after Christmas, the sea came over Frisia and 2,437 people were counted drowned.
This year the Frisians are said to have killed more than twelve thousand heathen men.
This year the Northmen laid waste Ostracia and Westracia: the one annal that names Westergo. The Danes took tribute and held nearly the whole province.
This year Rorik the Dane was given Dorestad and other counties. No text gives him Westergo.
This year 252 ships took payment in Frisia and went away.
This year the people newly called Cokingi drove Rorik out of Frisia.
This year in June Rodulf the Northman asked tribute of Count Albdag's Oostergo and fell there with five or eight hundred men; the Frisians were led by a Northman turned Christian.
In the later part of this century (?) more than 2,600 pennies, copies of the emperor Lothar's Dorestad coin, were buried at Tzummarum, a short walk north-east along the ridge.
history.source: L. van der Tuuk, Dorestad onthuld, Muntslag; nl.wikipedia Tzummarum

history.text: By about this year the dug part of the terp Tjitsma is no longer lived on, but the mound itself goes on growing to its greatest size in the next century.
From this year Liudolf of Brunswick is count in Westergo; under his son Bruno (1038-1057) pennies are struck at Bolsward, Dokkum, Leeuwarden and Stavoren.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Graafschap Midden-Friesland; Bruno II van Brunswijk

eras.text: A rich farm terp two generations after the Franks came. One leading house with its dependants, weaving huts full of looms, a smith, a bead bench when the bead man is in. No church: a priest comes when he comes. The old who saw the shrines burn are still alive, and in a hungry year the terp buys bread with cloth.

After the two hundred ships. The terp has paid its share once and knows it can be asked again. The law is written now and is quoted at the hearth. Landric the island priest says Mass at the cross by the old mound. Cloth goes south to the abbeys' collectors every autumn.

The flood years and the tribute years. Salt in the pits, fewer cattle, the mound raised by a layer of sods. In 846 the Northmen go through Westergo: on this terp silver is in the ground, not on the table, and strangers are watched from the top of the mound before they are greeted.

The Danes' years. Whoever holds Dorestad sends for his due, and pennies with a dead emperor's name are copied on this coast because everyone trusts them. Wells are dug on the terp. The pendants and knucklebones are no longer worn. In 867 the Frisians drive Rorik out; in 873 Rodulf dies in Oostergo.
Quieter. The sunken huts are gone and weaving is done in the houses. The children skate on bone. The old middle of the mound is given up for building, and the houses move outward as the terp grows.
A big terp village among dikes that are just beginning: a ring dike stands round Pingjum to the south. The creek is narrower every year. Cloth and stock still go out, by the Vlie and Stavoren.

The count is a Saxon lord from Brunswick whom nobody here has seen. His pennies come from Bolsward and Stavoren, and the terp's trade goes to those markets. The mound is at its greatest; what was a lords' seat is a village of free farmers who say so.

sites.name: The Ried bank
sites.see: A grey creek between banks of shining mud, sea lavender and glasswort on either side, the row of green mounds behind under a very large sky. Two small clinker boats lie on their bilges on a bed of hurdles. Curlews, wind, and the smell of mud and drying nets.
sites.source: The Ried may have kept an opening to the sea (Aalders et al., Paleo-aktueel 2004, after Vos 1999); boats grounding on its bank is a guess (?): the waterside was never dug.

sites.name: The foot of the mound
sites.see: Trodden turf at the foot of the terp where the cattle path comes down. When a boat is in, cloth is laid over a rail, cheeses stacked on a hide, and a folding scale hung from a spear shaft stuck in the ground. Children and dogs in front, the sod houses above against the light.
sites.source: No market is recorded (?). The goods are from the finds: Rhineland pottery in an unusually high share, Rhenish glass, iron bars, antler, amber, Carolingian pennies (Paleo-aktueel 1992-2004; JALC 2011).

sites.name: The head house
sites.see: A long low house with walls of stacked sods as thick as a man is tall and a reed roof smoking through the thatch. Inside it is dark and warm: cattle breathing at one end, a peat fire at the other, a bench along the wall, dice on a board. It smells of peat, wet wool and cows.
sites.source: One farmstead with a main house, outbuildings and sunken huts in every period; sod walls throughout (Paleo-aktueel 3-4; Gerrets et al. 1996). Not a king's hall: 'the lord's man', as wording_793.json has it. Dice and an antler tuning pin are in the finds (JALC 2011).

sites.name: The weaving huts
sites.see: Three small sheds dug knee-deep into the mound, their roofs hardly higher than a standing man. Through a door: an upright loom against the back wall, a row of clay weights swinging, two women passing the shuttle without looking. Damp, lanolin, and the knock of the sword beater.
sites.source: Sunken huts until about 850 with loom weights and spindle whorls gathered in them (JALC 2011; Paleo-aktueel 4). The law's screona, the weaving hut it is death to break into (Lex Frisionum, Additio I 3).

sites.name: The smith's floor
sites.see: An open-sided shed on the lee of the mound, its floor black and glittering with scale. A stone anvil block, a clay hearth, a boy at the bellows, bundles of iron bars from the north under the eave. Charcoal smoke, hot iron, and a keg of rivets by the door.
sites.source: A smithy floor of hammer-scale (Nijboer and Tulp 1997, an earlier period); iron forged from bars and scrap into the 10th century; 81 clench nails and roves from the 5th to the 9th century (Aalders et al. 2004).

sites.name: The bead bench
sites.see: A plank on two posts in the sun by the house wall. A thumb-sized clay cup of yellow glass over a little fire, an iron rod, a heap of raw amber and the flakes knapped off it, beads cooling in a bowl of ash. A man working with his tongue between his teeth.
sites.source: A crucible with yellow glass, a yellow mosaic cube and many yellow beads (Sablerolles 1994); raw amber knapped into beads on the terp (Paleo-aktueel 4); craftsmen who came and went (JALC 2011).

sites.name: The bare mound
sites.see: The second mound in the row, lower than the rest and grazed bare. At the top a square of darker grass where posts once stood, and a single thorn bush bent east by the wind. Sheep keep off the square. From here the whole marsh and the line of the sea can be seen.
sites.source: The game's (?), after the spine's hook for this port: no shrine has been found. The Franks burned the shrines in 734 (nl.wikipedia Slag aan de Boorne); Liudger broke more about 780 and the king took two thirds of the treasure (Altfrid I.16). The other six terps have never been dug.

sites.name: The cross on the terp
sites.see: An oak post a little taller than a man with a crosspiece pegged to it, set in the turf at the top of the head terp, grey already from the salt wind. A flat stone before it. When the priest is here he says Mass in the open with his back to the weather and his box on the stone.
sites.source: The game's (?): no church, saint or churchyard is recorded before the late-medieval St Andrew's. Christian by law: Sunday work costs 4 solidi, and a man in feud has peace in church (Lex Frisionum XVIII; Additio I 1). The priest Landric is the spine's (Altfrid I.22).

sites.name: The folds on the marsh
sites.see: Low sod walls on the salt grass below the mounds, hundreds of sheep moving like one thing, red cattle beyond them, a few small thick-necked horses. A herd boy with a long pole for jumping the creeks. Bleating, larks, and dung drying in stacks for the fire.
sites.source: The bone counts: sheep 2,881, cattle 1,601, horse 86 (Prummel et al., JALC 2011, table 3). A marsh without dikes, flooded at times (JALC; Frisia Coast Trail).

sites.name: The flats at low water
sites.see: Where the creek runs out the land simply stops being land: brown sand and mud to the edge of sight, stake nets standing dry, a man and a child small in the distance with a basket. Seals on a far bank. When the tide turns it comes in faster than a walk.
sites.source: Net-menders and fishers in the finds; a porpoise's skull and jaw (JALC 2011; Prummel et al. 2012). The tide at Harlingen is about 2 m today and the flats dry. 'The sand the tide covers' is where the law puts the robber of a shrine (Lex Frisionum, Additio XI).

sites.name: The sod well
sites.see: A round shaft lined with stacked sods and an old barrel sunk at the bottom, a hooked pole for the bucket, the turf round it worn to mud. Women waiting their turn with yokes, talking. The water tastes faintly of salt after a gale.
sites.source: Wells are mostly of 850-950 (JALC 2011; Haverkort et al. 1993).

people.name: Folcward
people.trait: Head of the leading house; careful, proud of what the terp was, and exact about what is owed.
people.want: To hand the house to his son with more sheep than he was given, and no Frank living on the mound.
people.fear: A bad year in which he must ask the count for bread and be told what it costs.
people.voice: Dry and slow. States a price as if it were weather. Never says a thing twice.
people.looks: About forty-five, tall and spare, fair hair gone thin, a clipped beard; a short blue-grey Frisian cloak pinned with a small round enamelled brooch, a knife with an antler handle, a tally stick.
knows: what cloth, cheese, hides and stock cost here this season, and what the terp will give for grain
the Frisians' law between Vlie and Lauwers: the wergilds, the solidus of three pennies
which count's man came last and what he asked
who on the seven mounds has silver and who only says so

ties.note: his brother's widow; she runs the looms and he sells what they make
his mother's brother, whom he houses and cannot make be quiet
a winter's iron work, to be paid in fleeces after shearing
knew his father; asks every skipper whether the steersman from Doccinga still sails
answers, at two removes, to the count's steward at Dorestad when the count remembers Westergo
she has bought the terp's cloth for twenty years and has never once been late with the silver
says the man on the Almere shore counts Winaldum bolts as longer than they are (?)
his son's son, born in his last year; the tally sticks will be his

lines.greet: A boat from the south. Come up out of the mud. Show us what you have. We are hoping for bread.
lines.greet_again: You again. The dogs knew your boat before I did. Sit down; the ale is no better than last time.
rumour: The count's man was here before shearing. He counted the sheep twice and got two numbers. We agreed on the smaller.
My uncle talks to the bare mound. I let him. It does not answer, so no law is broken.
They say the king is having our law written down. Then a Frank will be able to read me my own wergild.
lines.saying: Three pennies to the solidus on this side of the Vlie. Count it before you cross, not after.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb. And if you see grain cheaper than you sold it here, do not tell me.

people.source: invented; the leading family of the one farmstead is from Paleo-aktueel 3-4, the law from Lex Frisionum I, the enamelled disc brooch from Bos and Zijlstra 1996. Name: Folc- + -ward.

people.name: Liafburg
people.trait: A widow who runs three weaving huts and nine pairs of hands; quick, fair, and never idle while she talks.
people.want: Her daughter Wilburg married with her dowry silver whole; and one bolt of hers on a bishop's back.
people.fear: A hungry year that eats the dowry; and her own hands stiffening.
people.voice: Fast and plain, counts in bolts and ells, and judges a man by the cloth he has on.
people.looks: Near forty, small and strong, forearms like a rower's, hair under a linen cloth; a dress of her own grey-blue twill, a string of yellow beads, shears and a bone needle case at her belt.
knows: cloth: what is true Frisian twill and what is English wool sold under the name
what the abbeys' collectors take each autumn and what they leave
the law on the weaver's hand and on the weaving hut
every marriage talked of on the seven mounds

ties.note: her dead husband's brother; he sells, she makes, and she thinks he sells too cheap
the bead man made the yellow string she wears and is paid in cloth every summer
by marriage; she feeds him and scolds him
two widows who do their own counting; they have met twice and send each other word by every boat
wove the cloth for his Mass stone; he has promised to marry her daughter properly, before the cross
says the Oostergo women beat the weft too loose and then stretch the bolt (?)
Meinburg sells her grey cloth to the Rhine boats, and sends word of bad payers
the pilot hangs about her weaving huts; she has decided not to notice why
a cousin on the Ems; dye and gossip go between them by the same boats

lines.greet: That is an English cloak and a poor one. Stand in the light. I can do you better before the tide turns.
lines.greet_again: The one who can tell twill from sacking. Come in out of the wind; mind the weights.
rumour: The abbot's man takes his cloaks every autumn and calls it a gift. I have never yet been thanked by a saint.
Hurt my hand and the law gives me a quarter more than for another woman. It is the only time the law has noticed me.
They say the king himself complained our cloaks are too short. Let him pay for the long ones, then.
lines.saying: A bolt is a winter. Do not haggle with a winter.
lines.farewell: Keep it dry and folded, not rolled. And tell them at Dorestat whose it is.

people.source: invented; the weaving huts from JALC 2011, the weaver of fresum whose hurt hand costs a quarter more from Lex Frisionum, Additio II 24; Fulda's 855 Frisian cloaks a year about 830 (Frisia Coast Trail); the king on short cloaks from Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34. Name: Liaf- + -burg.

people.name: Aldward
people.trait: The oldest man on the mounds. Baptised twice, by his own count, and keeps sheep off one square of grass.
people.want: To be told, by someone who has seen it, what became of what was carried off from the bare mound.
people.fear: That when he is dead nobody will know where the posts stood.
people.voice: Flat and unhurried, without anger and without forgiveness. Tells a thing in the order it happened.
people.looks: Nearly seventy, bent, white hair and a long white moustache, pale eyes; an old undyed cloak, a herdsman's jumping pole twice his height, a worn sheep's knucklebone on a thong under his shirt.
knows: what stood on the bare mound, who burned it in his boyhood and who broke it again in his fiftieth year
the story of Finn and the fight in his hall, as the Frisians tell it
weather from the marsh: the smell before a flood tide
which ewe is whose, on all seven mounds

ties.note: his sister's son, who houses him
not a feud he would name: he watched Liudger's men carry the silver down to the boat, and Liudger spoke kindly to him
they knew the same stories of the old kings; the singer has not been west of the Lauwers in years
the island priest asks him the old names and does not scold him for knowing them
a cousin's daughter, he says, gone east long ago (?)
his bread, daily
a carter at the Danes' beach market whom he has never met: the marsh cattle he sends north go to him, and the tally sticks come back whole

lines.greet: Mind where you walk. Not the square. The sheep have learned it; a merchant can.
lines.greet_again: The one who walked round. Sit. I have nothing to sell you and a good deal to tell.
rumour: I was eight when the Franks burned it. We set the posts up again. Wood is cheap when it drifts in.
I was past fifty when the priest's men came with a boat. They weighed it on the grass. Two parts for the king, they said.
The priest himself was civil. He asked my name and used it. I have not decided what to think of that.
lines.saying: The sea gives the land and comes back for the rent.
lines.farewell: If you come to Traiectum, look at the bishop's cup. Tell me if it is ours. I only want to know.

people.source: invented, to carry the spine's hook (cross_and_grove): the burning of 734 is nl.wikipedia Slag aan de Boorne, the breaking about 780 and the king's two thirds Altfrid I.16; worn knucklebone amulets from JALC 2011. That either happened on this mound is the game's (?). Name: Ald- + -ward.

people.name: Bernrad
people.trait: The resident smith: patient, short of words, and unable to pass a boat without looking at her seams.
people.want: Good bar iron from the north without three men's profit on it; and a son who will stay at the bellows.
people.fear: Fire in the reed roofs with the wind in the west.
people.voice: A few words between hammer blows. Answers a question with what he would do about it.
people.looks: Thirty-three, broad and short, burned forearms, singed brown beard, a leather apron black with scale; tongs in one hand and a rove threaded on his little finger like a ring.
knows: a clinker hull: where she will leak next and how many rivets it will take
iron: which bars are northern and soft, which are Frankish and dear
what the smith at Doccinga charges, and why it is too much
who has brought scrap to be melted and did not say where it came from

ties.note: works on the head house's ground and is paid in fleeces and keep
mends his boat every spring and is paid in fish and talk
the bead man borrows his fire and gives back less charcoal than he took
says the Oostergo man sells rivets by the handful, not the count (?)
the Northman knows iron and has told him where the bars come from; Bernrad believes about half

lines.greet: She is weeping at the third strake. No, do not tell me; I can see it from here.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat. Then my rivets held. Bring her up on the hurdles and I will look.
rumour: Burn an old boat and rake the ash: that is where half my nails come from. Nothing is lost on a terp.
A man brought me a piece of gold foil to melt. From the plough, he said. I told him to plough there again.
Northern bars are dearer every year. The Danes' king takes his cut at one end and ours at the other.
lines.saying: A rivet is cheaper than a prayer and works in more weathers.
lines.farewell: Tar her before the frost, not after. And bring me bars if you go north.

people.source: invented; a resident smith (Paleo-aktueel 4), the clench nails and roves and the reading that old ship timber was burnt (Aalders et al. 2004), iron bars of Scandinavian kinds, the 7th-century gold foil die (Bos and Nijboer 1997). Name: Bern- + -rad.

people.name: Sicco
people.trait: Fisherman and pilot for the Vlie and the flats; cheerful, nosy, and never wrong about the tide.
people.want: A bigger boat than his brother-in-law's; and to be asked for by name at Dorestad.
people.fear: Fog on the flats with the flood making, which took his father.
people.voice: Talks all the time and loudly, as men do who work in wind. Measures everything in tides.
people.looks: Twenty-eight, lean and long-armed, red-brown from weather, bare legs muddy to the knee; a sealskin cap, a net needle of bone behind his ear, an eel spear over his shoulder.
knows: the channels of the Vlie and where the Ried still opens to the sea, tide by tide
what boats passed for the islands this month and whose they were
the price of fish, seal oil and a day's piloting
everything said on the creek bank, most of it true

ties.note: the smith keeps his boat alive
her daughter Wilburg, and the whole terp knows it but the mother will not
the steersman showed him the Lauwers channels one summer; Sicco tells it as if they were equals
they hand boats over at the Vlie mouth and each says the other's water is the easy half (?)
has met the Witla pilot once at Dorestad and quotes him ever since
his sister's son, whom he taught to count by notching the tides; the boy went east and became a factor

lines.greet: You came in on the wrong side of the stake. It does not matter today. It will matter at springs.
lines.greet_again: I saw your sail two tides ago and said so. Nobody believed me. Tell them it was you.
rumour: Three strange boats went north inside the islands at the last new moon. Long, low, no cargo showing. They did not ask the way.
The creek is narrower than in my father's day. The sea is building us a wall and will want paying for it.
We pulled a sea pig out of the nets at midsummer. The old man took its skull up to the mound. I did not ask.
lines.saying: The tide waits for the count as long as it waits for me.
lines.farewell: Ebb in the creek at first light. Keep the thorn bush over the stake and you will not touch.

people.source: invented; net-menders and fishers and the porpoise's skull from JALC 2011 and Prummel et al. 2012; the Ried opening from Aalders et al. 2004. Name: Sicco, a short form of a Sig- name (?).

people.name: Gerbrand
people.trait: A bead and comb maker who walks the terps from Easter to Martinmas; has been everywhere once and says so.
people.want: Yellow glass that stays yellow, raw amber by the sack, and a roof of his own for the winters.
people.fear: Being taken for a thief in a place where nobody will swear for him.
people.voice: Easy and joking, with a pedlar's habit of praising whatever you are looking at.
people.looks: About thirty-five, thin and stooped from the bench, quick stained fingers, a patched brown cloak hung with a dozen sample strings of beads; a pack frame, an iron rod, a comb in his hair.
knows: what beads, combs and amber fetch on every terp between the Vlie and the Ems
where the old gold turns up, and who quietly melts it
what silver is worth by weight against the king's new penny
news a season old from Dorestad and the Ems mouth

ties.note: she pays him in cloth and lets him sleep in a weaving hut
charcoal, by the smith's reckoning a cartload
a cousin on the Ems who buys his amber rough (?)
bought glass on trust at Dorestad and has paid half
sold him combs once at the Danes' market and was paid in a cut coin with strange writing

lines.greet: A man who has been somewhere. Good. Look at these while you tell me what amber costs there.
lines.greet_again: My best customer, or my most patient. The yellow ones came out well this time; see for yourself.
rumour: A ploughman two mounds along turned up a gold coin with a name on it. He thinks it is a button for a god.
The king has made his penny heavier. So now I am paid in fewer of them, and told it is the same.
I had a silver piece from the east set in a mount for a woman here. Writing like worm tracks. She likes it for that.
lines.saying: Glass is sand that met a careful man.
lines.farewell: I am here till the sheep come in. After that ask at the Ems mouth, or do not ask.

people.source: invented; the bead-maker (Sablerolles 1994), comb-sellers and goldsmiths who came and went (JALC 2011), amber knapped here and the dirham in a mount (Paleo-aktueel 4), the Audulf gold of about 600 (en.wikipedia Audulf), the reform of 793-794 (spine, silver_road). Name: Ger- + -brand.

people.name: Eilrad
people.trait: Folcward's grandson, head of the house through the flood and the tribute years; hard, fair, and tired of paying.
people.want: One year in which nobody comes by sea to be paid; failing that, to choose whom he pays.
people.fear: That the silver he has put in the ground will outlive everyone who knows where.
people.voice: Short. Asks who sent you before he asks what you sell. Laughs once a visit, late.
people.looks: Forty, heavy-shouldered, a scar through one eyebrow, grey in a cropped beard; a plain dark cloak with no brooch showing, a seax, and nothing on him that shines.
knows: who is taking tribute in Frisia this year, in whose name, and what was paid last time
which pennies are the emperor Lothar's own and which were struck on this coast, and that both are good silver
who drowned in the flood of Saint Stephen's day and whose land is empty
what the men called Cokingi are saying about Rorik

ties.note: his grandfather, whose tally sticks he still keeps
tribute, when Rorik's men can reach this far; he would not call it owing
sends worn pennies south to be weighed and trusts the answer (?)
the terps of Oostergo and Westergo send each other word when sails are seen (?)
believes someone on the Almere shore tells the Danes which terps have had a good year (?)

lines.greet: Say whose boat she is and who told you to come here. Good. Then come up. We look first, these years.
lines.greet_again: You are the one who comes back. That is rarer than silver now. Sit by the fire.
rumour: They burned Westergo from end to end in my thirty-fourth year. We were on the marsh with the sheep. The sods do not burn well.
The pennies with Lothar's name are still being struck, and he is dead. A dead emperor asks no tribute; people trust him.
There is a new word going round the terps. Cokingi. Ask what it means and you will be asked whose side you are on.
lines.saying: Pay a Dane once and you have a custom. Pay him twice and you have a lord.
lines.farewell: Go inside the islands. And if you are asked what we have here, we have sheep.

people.source: invented; the flood of 838, the wasting of Westracia in 846, Rorik in 850 and the Cokingi of 867 from the annals of Xanten and St Bertin; the copied Lothar pennies and the Tzummarum hoard from L. van der Tuuk, Dorestad onthuld. Name: Eil- + -rad.

stories.title: The bare mound
stories.summary: An old herdsman saw the shrine on the second mound burned by the Franks when he was a boy and broken again by Liudger's men when he was past fifty. He does not want it back: he wants to know, from someone who has seen, what became of the silver.
stories.picture: An old man with a tall pole standing beside a square of darker grass on a bare green mound, a bent thorn bush behind him, sheep keeping their distance, the sea a line at the edge of the sky.

beats.text: Aldward tells it in order: the fire in 734, the posts set up again, the priest's boat about 780, the silver weighed on the grass, two parts for the king and one for the bishop. He asks you to look at the bishop's cup at Traiectum.

The keeper of Saint Martin's treasure will show the plate to a man who gives alms. One cup has a band of old work under the rim: animals biting their own backs, not Frankish. Nobody there knows where it came from, only that it came in Bishop Alberic's day.
Bernlef knew the mound and gives its old name; Liudger, if asked plainly, says the king's share went to the king and he has never asked where. He remembers the boy with the sheep, who was not a boy.

Landric the island priest wants to set a cross on the bare mound itself, not beside it, and asks the merchant to speak to the old man first, since he will listen to a stranger sooner than to a priest.
You come back with what you saw. He listens to the end without a word.

endings.how: You looked at the cup and told him exactly what you saw, no more.
endings.text: He says: then it is drinking wine for a bishop, and that is at least a use. He walks you round the square once and names each post. After his death the house keeps sheep off it for another forty years.
endings.reward: Aldward as a fast friend; the story of Finn told to the end (give_text beowulf_16 and beowulf_17); a standing welcome at the head house.

endings.how: You spoke for Landric and the cross was set on the bare mound.
endings.text: Aldward does not come up the mound again. Landric says Mass there every time he passes, and Liafburg's daughter is married before it. The old man is buried, by his own word, on the flats side.
endings.reward: Landric and Liafburg as friends; the terp counts as Christian in earnest (hear_mass and sanctuary at the cross from that year); a deed the church remembers.

endings.how: You never went to Traiectum and told him the silver had been given to the poor.
endings.text: He looks at you for some time and says the poor must be very well dressed at Traiectum. He does not hold it against you; he does not speak of the mound to you again.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but his talk: his rumours and the Finn story are closed to this merchant.

stories.reward: A friend for life on the terp and the old stories in the chest, or the priest's friendship and a cross on the mound: not both.

stories.title: Bread for cloth
stories.summary: The terp country grows cattle, not corn. In the hungry years a boat with grain is the most welcome thing on the creek, and the terp will pay in cloth, cheese, hides or, when those are gone, a daughter's dowry silver.
stories.picture: Sacks of grain being carried up the cattle path from a small boat on the mud, a woman at the top of the mound holding a folded bolt of grey-blue cloth in both arms, thin children watching the sacks.

beats.text: Thiadburg sells her grain at the king's price and says the terps to the north will be eating their seed barley by Easter. Thiadbod, who is holding his, says the same and smiles.
Folcward will not beg. He names what the terp can give for a sack: cloth first, then cheese and hides. The silver is nearly gone. Liafburg stands behind him and says nothing, which is not like her.
Liafburg, alone, offers her daughter Wilburg's dowry: old pennies, a gold pendant, the yellow beads. It would buy the whole cargo above the king's price. She asks only that Folcward not be told.
A good year. The debt, if there is one, is paid in new cloth without being asked for, and the merchant is given the bench by the fire.

endings.how: You sold at the king's price and took cloth, cheese and hides for it.
endings.text: The terp eats until the grass comes. Liafburg sets aside the first bolt off her loom for you every year after, and says whose it is at the foot of the mound.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor; the unlock wijnaldum.first_bolt; Folcward and Liafburg friendly; the cargo of cloth sells at Dorestad for about a quarter over what the grain cost.

endings.how: You left the grain on Folcward's tally stick, to be paid after shearing.
endings.text: He cuts the notches deep and breaks the stick with you. After shearing the debt is paid in full and a bolt over. A tally kept through a famine is remembered for a generation.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor; a third more cloth than the grain was worth, a season late; the unlock wijnaldum.hearth_seat.

endings.text: It is a good price and nobody starves. Wilburg's wedding waits three years. Liafburg sells you cloth afterwards as she would to any stranger, and Sicco the pilot suddenly cannot find the time to take you out.
endings.reward: About 300 pennies' worth of old silver and a gold pendant with four runes on it; Liafburg cool; sets hy_sold_dear if the count's men hear of it.

stories.reward: A terp that remembers who fed it, or a bag of old silver and a closed door.

stories.title: The terp's share
stories.summary: In the summer of 810 two hundred Danish ships lie on the islands, three fights are lost, and each terp is told its share of the hundred pounds. Winaldum's is two pounds by weight (?), due before the next spring tide, and the terp has cloth, not silver.
stories.picture: A folding scale hanging from a spear shaft at the foot of the mound, a heap of pennies, hack-silver and a woman's beads beside it, grim men in short cloaks watching the pan, long ships small and dark out on the flats.

beats.text: Sails seen inside the islands, more than can be counted from a small boat. Sicco, if he is aboard as pilot, counts them anyway and stops at sixty.

If you bring warning before the fleet's men come (flag gf_warned), the cattle are driven inland and the cloth is sunk in the creek in tarred hides. If not, the Danes' counter has already been and gone and the number is fixed.

The share is weighed in the open. Everything silver on the seven mounds is in the pan and it is a third short. Folcward asks, as a thing between merchants, what you have aboard and what you would want for it.
News that Godfred is dead by his own man's hand, and peace sworn on the Eider. Folcward pays what he owes, or remembers that he was not helped.
The toll man on the Almere shore has weighed his own row's share and found it short. He asks what Winaldum was told to find.

endings.how: You made up the weight from your own silver and asked nothing.
endings.text: The ships leave on the next tide. Folcward says nothing at all, which from him is a great deal, and has your name cut on his tally of things owed that cannot be paid.
endings.reward: Sets gf_paid_share; the unlock wijnaldum.hearth_seat for this merchant and his heir; cloth at the terp's own price for ten years.

endings.how: You lent the silver against next year's cloth.
endings.text: It is business and both sides know it. The cloth comes, every bolt, and it is good. You are thanked exactly as much as you were owed.
endings.reward: Sets gf_paid_share; the loan back half again in cloth by the next Martinmas; Folcward easy, no more.

endings.how: You sailed on the ebb with your silver aboard.
endings.text: The terp pays in cattle and two men's sons as hostages until the rest is found. They come home in 811. Nobody is rude to you afterwards; nobody remembers your name either.
endings.reward: Your silver, whole. Feeling at Winaldum falls, and the story is told at Doccinga before you get there.

endings.how: You brought warning in time (gf_warned), whatever you did after.
endings.text: The best of the stock and the cloth were out of sight when the counter came, and the share was set lower for it. Sicco tells this story for the rest of his life, with himself in it.
endings.reward: The share is a quarter less; Sicco pilots you free of charge from then on (the unlock wijnaldum.vlie_marks).

stories.reward: A debt of honour on a terp that keeps tallies for three generations.

stories.title: Silver in the sod
stories.summary: From 846 whoever holds the rivers sends north for tribute. Eilrad puts the terp's silver in the ground, pennies with the dead emperor Lothar's name on them, and needs one outsider who knows where, because everyone on the mound who knows could drown in one night.
stories.picture: Two men at dusk kneeling at the foot of a sod wall with a small grey pot between them, one holding back the turf like a lid, the low sun red on the marsh and a single sail far out.

beats.text: At Dorestad they say the Danes have been through Ostracia and Westracia and hold nearly the whole province. A moneyer shows a penny of Lothar's that was never struck in his mint, and shrugs: the silver is good.

Eilrad asks who sent you, then feeds you. On the third visit he shows you a pot and a place. He asks one thing: if the house is empty when you next come, dig it up and take it to his sister's son at Doccinga.
Rorik's men come for the due. They ask the merchant, pleasantly, whether this terp has had a good year.
The Cokingi have driven Rorik out. At Doccinga they are counting who paid and who was paid. Eilrad's nephew wants to know whether the pot is still where it was.

endings.how: You said the terp had sheep, and left the pot where it lay.
endings.text: In 867 Eilrad digs it up himself and counts it in front of you. He gives you one penny in twelve, which he calls the keeper's share and says is old law. It is not, but it is his.
endings.reward: About 200 pennies in good imitation Lothar coin; Eilrad as a fast friend; your heir is greeted by name on this terp.

endings.how: The house stood empty after a raid, and you dug up the pot and carried it to Doccinga.
endings.text: The nephew weighs it twice and finds it whole. The house at Winaldum is rebuilt with it the next spring, and a bench in it is yours.
endings.reward: A tenth of the silver as the carrier's due; the unlock wijnaldum.hearth_seat; friends in both Westergo and Oostergo.

endings.how: You told Rorik's men it had been a very good year.
endings.text: They find the pot in an afternoon. You are paid a finder's part and sail the same tide. Another pot, at Tzummarum along the ridge, is never found by anyone until a farmer's plough.
endings.reward: About 400 pennies at once; shunned at Winaldum and cool on every terp where the story is told; Rorik's men remember you kindly.

stories.reward: A keeper's share and a name that outlasts you here, or quick silver and a coast that closes.

stories.title: The weaver's hand
stories.summary: A man breaks into a weaving hut at night for the cloth and, caught, crushes a weaver's hand in the door. The law has a price for each: his life or its ransom for the hut, and for the hand a quarter more than another woman's. The terp needs a witness who is nobody's kin.
stories.picture: A firelit sod house full of standing people, a bound man on his knees, a woman with her right hand wrapped in linen held up for all to see, an elder with a tally stick between them.

beats.text: A stranger sells you, or offers you, a bolt of grey-blue twill a good deal under its worth. One selvedge has a yellow thread in it.
Liafburg knows her own selvedge across a field. One of her women has a crushed hand. The man is held in the head house and says he bought the cloth honestly at Medemelacha.
The case is heard by the hearth, the law said aloud from memory: break into a weaving hut and it is your life, or buy it back. A stranger's oath weighs here, because he has no cousin on either side.
At Aalsum the weavers have heard of the crushed hand, and of the law's quarter more for it. Meinhild says a hand is not paid for in quarters.

endings.how: You swore to what you saw at Medemelacha.
endings.text: The man buys back his life with all he has and his kin's besides, and the weaver is paid her quarter more. She weaves again by the next summer, slower.
endings.reward: Liafburg as a fast friend and the unlock wijnaldum.first_bolt; a deed of honest witness; the thief's kin at Medemelacha cool.

endings.how: You swore to it and then offered part of the ransom yourself.
endings.text: The terp thinks you soft and the thief's kin think you a saint; both will deal with you. The man works three years at Folcward's folds and stays on after.
endings.reward: Costs about 60 pennies; friends at Medemelacha and no enemy here; a herdsman who will always say what stock is really worth.

endings.how: You said you could not be sure of the selvedge.
endings.text: Without a witness it goes to the lot: two sticks on the cross stone, one marked. The lot clears him. Liafburg sells you no more cloth with a yellow thread in it.
endings.reward: No cost and no gain; Liafburg wary.

stories.reward: The best cloth on the coast before anyone else sees it, and a name for a straight oath.

stories.title: The cousins' dye
stories.summary: Liafburg of Winaldum has the red and her cousin Tetta on the Ems has the blue, and for twenty years they have traded dye and gossip by other people's boats. A house that carries for both is told what each says of the other, and is sold cloth by both at the price they give kin.
stories.picture: Two hands across a boat's gunwale: a woman's with red-stained fingers passing a sewn sack to a man's; in the background, small, another woman on another shore with arms blue to the elbow.

beats.text: Liafburg sews a sack of madder shut, twice, and gives it to you for her cousin on the Ems. She says Tetta's blue is the best on the coast, and that you are not to tell her so.
Tetta cuts the stitches, smells the madder, and makes up a bundle of woad in return, with a message in words you are not meant to understand.
Liafburg unties the woad, complains of the knots, and sells you two bolts at forty.

endings.how: You carried the madder east and the woad back west.
endings.text: The two widows go on quarrelling by way of your boat for as long as they live. Each asks what the other said. You learn to say less than you were told.
endings.reward: Frisian cloth at forty pennies the bolt at Winaldum; both weavers friendly; the deed kept_commission.

endings.how: You took the madder and never called at the Ems.
endings.text: The sack goes mouldy under your deck boards. Liafburg asks once. Then she sends her dye by another boat, and sells you cloth at the strand's price.
endings.reward: Nothing; the weaver's good word lost.

stories.reward: Cloth at the kin price at both ends of the Frisian coast, and the best gossip between the Vlie and the Ems.

works.name: A hurdle hard on the creek
works.what: Wattle hurdles and brushwood pegged down over the mud of the Ried bank with oak stakes, so that a loaded boat can be grounded and worked dry-shod at any state of the tide.
works.needs: Folcward's leave (or his heir's), and a visit in the dry of summer.
works.gives: Loading and careening here take half the time; a boat on the hard is safe in a gale that would strain her on the mud.
works.picture: Men laying woven hurdles on shining mud beside a grounded boat, stakes being driven with a wooden maul.
works.source: The game's (?): no landing is known and the waterside was never dug. Hurdle and brushwood hards are the ordinary landing of the period's beach markets.

works.name: A store hut of your own
works.what: A small shed dug knee-deep into the flank of the terp, walled with sods and roofed with reed, like the weaving huts beside it; breaking into such a hut is a matter of life by the Frisians' law.
works.needs: To be known on the terp: three visits, or the hearth seat.
works.gives: Goods can be left here between voyages (store); cloth bought over a summer can wait for one cargo.
works.picture: A low reed roof hardly rising from the slope of the mound, a plank door with a wooden lock, bolts of cloth just visible inside.
works.source: Sunken huts until about 850 (JALC 2011; Paleo-aktueel 4); Lex Frisionum, Additio I 3 on the screona.

works.name: A layer on the mound
works.what: After the flood of Saint Stephen's day the terp is raised by a spade's depth of fresh sods over the whole head mound and its cattle path, every household carrying, as the mounds have always been raised.
works.needs: The winter after a flood; the head of the house must agree, and the work is done between hay and harvest.
works.gives: The terp's stock and stores come through the next flood year whole; the house remembers who paid for the carrying.
works.picture: A line of men, women and children with sods on carrying boards climbing a green mound, drowned grey marsh all round.
works.source: The terp begun as a sod platform and raised period by period (Paleo-aktueel 3; JALC 2011); the flood of 26 December 838 (chronicle_793.json); a ring dike round Pingjum in the 10th century.

works.name: A well on the terp
works.what: A shaft sunk through the mound to sweet water and lined with stacked sods, an old cask set at the bottom to keep it open.
works.needs: An old wine cask to give, and a dry month.
works.gives: Water can be taken here without sending to the pools (provision is quicker); the women at the well tell you the news first.
works.picture: A man waist-deep in a round hole stacking sods, a cask waiting beside it, women with yokes looking on.
works.source: Wells mostly of 850-950 (JALC 2011; Haverkort et al. 1993). Cask-lined wells are known from Dorestad (?).

works.name: A roof for the cross
works.what: A small house of posts and sods with a reed roof built over the cross on the head terp, so that the priest need not say Mass in the rain. Nothing of the kind has been found here: this one is the merchant's doing.
works.needs: Landric's asking, or a later priest's, and the head of the house not against it.
works.gives: Mass is said here whenever a priest passes; a man in feud has peace under its roof; the bishop at Traiectum hears whose silver built it.
works.picture: A tiny sod-walled building with a wooden cross on its gable on top of a green mound, a priest in a sealskin cloak at the door.
works.source: The game's (?): no church is recorded at Wijnaldum before St Andrew's of about 1500. A man in feud has peace in church: Lex Frisionum, Additio I 1.

ships.note: A fisher's clinker boat off the creek bank, sold when a man dies or goes into another's boat. The terp's own boats are this size.
ships.picture: A small tarred clinker boat lying on her bilge on the mud with nets drying over her side.
ships.source: Net-menders and fishers (JALC 2011); the authors of the nail study hold that Frisians of these centuries sailed clinker boats (Aalders et al. 2004).

ships.note: Now and then a six-oar clinker boat of the northern kind changes hands here; the smith can re-rivet her from his own keg. Whether boats were built on the terp is not known (?).
ships.picture: A slim six-oar boat hauled out on hurdles, the smith crouched at her strakes with a hammer and a dolly.
ships.source: 81 clench nails and roves of the 5th to 9th century, from repairs or old ship timber burnt (Aalders et al. 2004).

ships.note: In autumn the boat that takes the cloaks owed to the abbeys can be hired for the run south, with her steersman, if she is not full (?).
ships.picture: A beamy beach-landing boat loaded with bundled cloth under hides, pushing off from a marsh creek in grey weather.
ships.source: Fulda drew 855 Frisian cloaks a year about 830 (Frisia Coast Trail, after the Fulda rent lists); how they travelled is not recorded (?).

sayings.text: Hurt the hand of a harper, a goldsmith or a woman who weaves Frisian cloth, and you pay a quarter more than for another's. The law knows whose hands feed the country.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum, Additio II 23-24 (our rendering, after K. Nieuwenhuijsen)

sayings.text: The king looked at a Frisian cloak and asked what use such a little rag was: it would not cover him in bed, nor on a horse in the rain. On the terps they say the king has never had to weave one.
sayings.source: After Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (Grant 1907 is the public-domain English; our wording); the reply is invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Hávamál 77 (Bellows 1923; stanza 76 in other editions) (?): said here by northern traders, and thought sound by people who count their wealth in cattle

sayings.text: The sea gives the land and comes back for the rent.
A terp is what a man owes his grandfather, with a layer on it for his grandson.
We grow everything here except bread, wood and iron. Otherwise we want for nothing.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the terp country's want of corn is the spine's (hungry_years)

sayings.text: A riddle asked at the hearth: I stand all winter against the wall with stones hanging from my hair; a woman beats me with a sword and I grow longer for it. Say what I am. (A loom.)
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the Exeter riddles; compare riddles_793.json 'loom'

sayings.text: A Frank asked the way to the king of the Frisians. He was shown a sheep. It was the oldest thing there with a following.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: there is no Frisian king after 734 (wording_793.json)

easter_eggs.text: Somewhere in the clay of the head terp lies a gold brooch as long as a hand and a half, set with more than three hundred red stones that came from the far side of the world. Nobody alive knows it is there. Its foot will be turned up by a farmer in 1953 and spend a while on his sister's window sill.
easter_eggs.source: nl.wikipedia Fibula van Wijnaldum; Frisia Coast Trail, Ornament of the gods; garnets traced to India in 2012

easter_eggs.text: The bead man's ploughman has a small gold coin that reads AVDVLFVS FRISIA. No one on the terp can read it, and no one remembers an Audulf.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia Audulf; a die naming him is said to have been found here in 2006 (?) (fy.wikipedia Terp Tsjitsma)

easter_eggs.text: The gold pendant in Wilburg's dowry has four runes scratched on it. Ravn reads them slowly: hiwi. The woman of the house.
easter_eggs.source: Looijenga and Zijlstra, Paleo-aktueel 1992: a gold pendant of about 600, read hiwi, 'mother of the household', or as a name

easter_eggs.text: On the bench in the head house lies a flute somebody began to cut from a sheep's shin and never finished: three holes marked, one bored.
easter_eggs.source: Prummel et al., JALC 3 (2011): an unfinished flute of sheep's tibia, 750-850

easter_eggs.text: A sea pig's skull, bleached white, sits in the grass at the edge of the square on the bare mound. Nobody admits to putting it there.
easter_eggs.source: Prummel, Van Gent, Kompanje 2012: a porpoise's skull and jaw from the terp, 750-850; its place on the mound is the game's

easter_eggs.text: The bead man keeps one small yellow cube of glass that he did not make and will not sell: it came, he says, out of a wall in a city of the Romans.
easter_eggs.source: Sablerolles 1994: a yellow mosaic tessera among the glass-working waste

easter_eggs.text: In a hard winter after 850 the children cross the frozen creek on skates made from the leg bones of horses, pushing themselves with a spiked stick.
easter_eggs.source: Prummel et al., JALC 3 (2011): bone skates in the last phase

easter_eggs.text: In the oldest corner of the mound, the herdsman says, two foals that were never born lie buried one on the other, laid down with care and not thrown to the dogs. He does not know why and will not have it dug.
easter_eggs.source: Haverkort et al., Paleo-aktueel 1993: two unborn foals buried together, Migration period

easter_eggs.text: The smith's floor glitters because it is made of his grandfathers' work: scale off the anvil trodden in for longer than anyone has counted.
easter_eggs.source: Nijboer and Tulp, Paleo-aktueel 1997: a smithy floor of hammer-scale, dated 136-386

unlocks.what: The first bolt off Liafburg's looms each year
unlocks.how: Sell grain at the king's price in a hungry year, or bear true witness in the matter of the weaver's hand.
unlocks.gives: Frisian cloth here at the maker's price before the market opens (buy_at_source at the weaving huts, about a sixth under the port's price); npc feeling of the weaver at friendly or better.

unlocks.what: A seat at the head house's fire
unlocks.how: Carry the terp through 810, keep a tally through a famine, or bring the buried silver safe to Doccinga.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging (lodge), the house's news before the creek's (ask_news), and a welcome that passes to the merchant's heir at half strength, as feeling does.

unlocks.what: Sicco's marks for the Vlie and the Ried
unlocks.how: Hire Sicco three times, or bring warning of the fleet in 810.
unlocks.gives: No pilot is needed between the Almere and Winaldum (learn); the creek can be entered on a falling tide without touching.

unlocks.what: The fight at Finn's hall, as an old Frisian tells it
unlocks.how: Tell Aldward the truth about the silver from the bare mound.
unlocks.gives: give_text beowulf_16 and beowulf_17; a later card can ask what the merchant was told.

unlocks.how: Bring Bernrad northern bar iron twice at a fair price.
unlocks.gives: Repairs here on credit until the next visit, and fit_upgrade work done first, ahead of the terp's own boats.

unlocks.how: Know where Eilrad's pot lies and say nothing until 867.
unlocks.gives: One penny in twelve of the terp's silver (silver), and Eilrad's oath spoken for the merchant on any terp in Westergo.
